newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Manuel steps up pre-budget S.Africa charm campaign.
newsitem.headline: Manuel steps up pre-budget S.Africa charm campaign.

text.p: South African Finance Minister Trevor Manuel stepped up a pre-budget charm offensive on Thursday, promising nervous markets fiscal rectitude and further economic reforms.
With less than three weeks to go before arguably the most important budget of the post-apartheid era, Manuel has abandoned the usual cloak of silence ahead of his March 12 speech to parliament.

Instead, he and Reserve Bank Governor Chris Stals have had a hectic week briefing local and international investors on the improving economic situation in South Africa, including a sharply narrowing current account deficit.

Addressing the first-ever domestic roadshow on Thursday, Manuel once again pledged his commitment to the "main plank" of the government's Growth, Employment and Redistribution (GEAR) strategy -- grinding down the budget deficit.
"The four percent deficit for 1997/98 is immutable," he said, referring the promise in GEAR to cut the deficit from 5.1 percent this year to 4.0 percent in 1997/98 and 3.0 by the end of the decade.
Manuel said the government would achieve this target without including privatisation receipts -- prompting spontaneous applause from the audience of bond traders and economists.

South African government bonds took heart from the deficit pledge, moving to their best levels in a year. But the rand remained nervous after stalling below the 4.40 level against the dollar last week. Since then the currency has been volatile, trading around 4.48 on Thursday.
Currency dealers say investors are on edge ahead of the budget, seen as a key test of the African National Congress government's commitment to delivering reform after the rand's collapse in 1996.

Attention is focused, in particular, on the next step in the gradual easing of exchange controls -- something the markets welcome in principle but which at the same time raises fears of a damaging flight of capital.
Stals said earlier this week that next move in relaxing capital controls could include private individuals, but he stressed that any moves would not be spectacular.
Manuel said on Thursday that a lot of work was in progress on controls, but gave no further details.
Economists said the authorities appeared to be softening the markets up for an imminent exchange control announcement in or around the budget in the hope that when it comes the impact will be muted.

Ironically, while the markets appear to have warmed to Manuel -- who also promised this week to bring the government debt to GDP ratio down to 55 percent from 58 percent in 1997 -- Stals, a long-time favourite, has come in for some criticism.

His suggestion on two occasions in the last two weeks that the recent rapid rise in the rand -- though not the absolute level of the currency -- may have been overdone has unnerved the market, burning players in the process.
Stals' concern is on the impact of a stronger rand on the vital export sector of the economy, the main driver of what is expected to be modest economic growth in 1997.
